notes.1a: Credit for this part was awarded for clear explanation. Most candidates commenced by giving appropriate units for power or energy. In some cases the subsequent working and cancellations to give the result were unclear. Candidates should be reminded that it is especially important for the working to be clear in this type of question as credit is not awarded for the final answer.
notes.1b: (i) Having written down all the units for the various components, the subsequent working was not always clear. It was common to find that the conclusion reached was ‘1 = 1’ or ‘0 = 0’.
notes.1bii: In most scripts, the calculation of the intensity in W m –2 was completed successfully. Candidates found it more difficult to convert to pW m , and many stated the answer without conversion.

notes.3a: (i) 1. This calculation caused very few problems. Candidates should be advised always to use the given data, unless told otherwise. The approximation g = 10 m s should be avoided. 2. It was expected that candidates would use ideas related to conservation of energy and hence equate the maximum kinetic energy to the change in gravitational potential energy. In practice, most correctly calculated the final speed and then used the expression EK = ½mv .
notes.3aii: Very few answers included both a statement and some explanation. The most common answer was a statement without explanation to the effect that the velocity increases with time. It was expected that a reference would be made to velocity being proportional to time elapsed because the acceleration is constant.
notes.3iii: A small number of candidates made a correct reference to the fact that, at a speed of 60 m s –1 , the air resistance is less than the weight. Most attempted an unsuccessful explanation based on the fact that the graph extends beyond 60 m s .
notes.3b: (i) Generally, it was stated that the air resistance would increase as the velocity increases, giving rise to a reducing acceleration. Often there was no reference to the resultant force or there was a statement that the final acceleration would be zero.
notes.3bii: Candidates found this difficult. The most common mistake was to assume that the force due to air resistance was the accelerating force.
notes.4a: (i) Many candidates correctly considered the component of the force and used this correctly to determine the reaction force.
notes.4aii: As in (a)(i), a correct solution was seen in most scripts. The most common mistake was not to use the horizontal component of the force.
notes.4b: (i) This question concerned work done, but very few answers involved energy. In many answers there was some discussion of forces in equilibrium.
notes.4bii: Candidates should be encouraged to use terms such as ‘equal and opposite’, rather than ‘cancels out’ or ‘balanced’. The use of imprecise terminology frequently meant that credit could not be given.
notes.5a: (i) A very common error was to assume that resistance is the gradient of a voltage/current graph. This is a common misconception and candidates would benefit from further emphasis on the definition of resistance. Those who did recognise resistance as the ratio V/I frequently wrote that zero current would be associated with zero resistance.

notes.key_messages:
• There are a number of questions on the paper that require general recall. Candidates should review the
learning objectives and ensure they are well prepared to give correct answers to this type of question.
• Candidates should be reminded that, where a question asks for a statement and an explanation, the
explanation is essential to receive full credit. Credit is frequently lost when candidates do not show a
clear link between the stages in an argument.
• Candidates should choose their wording carefully, especially when giving a definition or describing a
situation. Often answers are made unclear through the omission of certain key words and inappropriate
use of everyday language.
• It is important that numerical answers are fully worked out and presented as decimals and not fractions.
Candidates should be reminded that full credit is not awarded for answers inappropriately given as
fractions.
notes.general_comments:
There were parts of some questions that were testing, allowing well-prepared candidates to show their
understanding of the relevant concepts. Other parts of questions were straightforward so that weaker
candidates would not be discouraged.
Candidates generally performed better on the questions involving calculations. Answers that required some
discussion or explanation were often not as well answered.
Some candidates did not answer all parts of all questions. However, there was no evidence that an
adequately prepared candidate had insufficient time to complete the answers.
